claims.text: A conventionally cast and homogenized CrCoNi- or AlCoCrFeNi-based HEA can provide a single-phase baseline with moderate strength and ductility.
Controlled cold or warm rolling will induce deformation nanotwins in the selected HEA.
A tuned annealing or ageing treatment after rolling will precipitate fine, coherent second-phase particles.
The proposed thermomechanical sequence will transform the single-phase starting material into a dual-phase or duplex nanostructure with elevated interface density.
Tailored thermomechanical processing can produce an ultrafine duplex microstructure in an AlCoCrFeNi-based eutectic HEA.
Nanoscale twins and coherent precipitates obstruct dislocation motion.
Nanoscale twins and coherent precipitates provide sites for strain partitioning.
The proposed obstacles delay dislocation accumulation.
The engineered heterogeneous microstructure delays crack initiation or propagation.
A duplex or hierarchically heterogeneous HEA microstructure can improve the strength-ductility combination.
The proposed twin-and-precipitate architecture will increase Young's modulus relative to the conventionally processed alloy.
Nanostructured HEAs can combine high specific yield strength, good ductility, and high Young's modulus.
The treated alloy may exhibit more than a 50% increase in yield and tensile strengths relative to the baseline.
The treated alloy will exhibit greater uniform elongation than the baseline.
The treated alloy will exhibit a modest increase in Young's modulus.
The treated alloy will exhibit enhanced fracture toughness because crack propagation is delayed.
Conventionally processed single-phase HEAs generally face a strength-ductility trade-off.
Inherently brittle alloys or alloys that form coarse, non-coherent precipitates may not benefit from this processing strategy.
Extreme service temperatures may eliminate the benefits by compromising nanotwin stability or precipitate coherence.

contradictions.description: The prediction calls for more than 50% improvement only in strength and merely a modest modulus increase, whereas the falsification rule appears to require a 20–30% enhancement across all targeted properties, including modulus, ductility, and fracture toughness.
